description: Using a 555 timer in astable mode: calculating frequency, period and mark-space ratio.
content_html:
From One-Shot to Continuous Oscillation

The previous lesson showed how the 555 timer in monostable mode fires a single timed pulse when triggered. In astable mode, there is no stable state at all — the output switches continuously between HIGH and LOW, producing a repeating waveform without any external trigger. This makes the 555 astable a simple and reliable oscillator, used in LED flashers, alarm sounders, clock pulse generators and many other applications.

The Astable Circuit

The 555 astable uses two external resistors (\(R_1\) and \(R_2\)) and one capacitor (\(C\)). The capacitor charges through both \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) in series, but discharges through only \(R_2\). This asymmetry means the time the output spends HIGH is longer than the time it spends LOW, producing a waveform where the mark time and space time are different.

The timing equations for the two half-cycles are:

  • Time HIGH (mark time): \(T_{ON} = 0.7 \times (R_1 + R_2) \times C\)
  • Time LOW (space time): \(T_{OFF} = 0.7 \times R_2 \times C\)

Period and Frequency

The total period of one complete cycle is the sum of the two half-cycles: \(T = T_{ON} + T_{OFF}\). Substituting the expressions above:

Key Fact

555 astable frequency:

$$f = \frac{1.44}{(R_1 + 2R_2) \times C}$$

where \(f\) is in hertz, \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) are in ohms, and \(C\) is in farads. Note that \(R_2\) is multiplied by 2, not \(R_1\).

Period \(T = 1/f\). You can also find the period directly:

$$T = 0.7 \times (R_1 + 2R_2) \times C$$

Mark-Space Ratio

Mark-space ratio (sometimes called mark-to-space ratio) describes the shape of the output waveform:

$$\text{Mark-space ratio} = \frac{T_{ON}}{T_{OFF}} = \frac{R_1 + R_2}{R_2}$$

Because the capacitor charges through both \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) but discharges through only \(R_2\), \(T_{ON}\) is always greater than \(T_{OFF}\) when \(R_1 > 0\). This means the mark-space ratio is always greater than 1 in a standard 555 astable. A mark-space ratio of 1:1 (equal HIGH and LOW times) is called a 50% duty cycle. The standard 555 astable cannot achieve exactly 50% duty cycle unless \(R_1 = 0\) Ω (which would damage the IC), so a modified circuit using a diode is needed for a 1:1 ratio.

A 555 astable has \(R_1 = 10\) kΩ, \(R_2 = 47\) kΩ and \(C = 100\) nF. Calculate the frequency and mark-space ratio.

Step 1 — Convert units to SI base units:

\(R_1 = 10 \times 10^{3} = 10{,}000\) Ω; \(R_2 = 47 \times 10^{3} = 47{,}000\) Ω; \(C = 100 \times 10^{-9}\) F.

Step 2 — Calculate the denominator:

\(R_1 + 2R_2 = 10{,}000 + 2 \times 47{,}000 = 10{,}000 + 94{,}000 = 104{,}000\) Ω

Step 3 — Substitute into the frequency formula:

$$f = \frac{1.44}{104{,}000 \times 100 \times 10^{-9}} = \frac{1.44}{104{,}000 \times 10^{-7}} = \frac{1.44}{0.0104} \approx 138\text{ Hz}$$

Step 4 — Mark-space ratio:

$$\text{Mark-space ratio} = \frac{R_1 + R_2}{R_2} = \frac{10{,}000 + 47{,}000}{47{,}000} = \frac{57{,}000}{47{,}000} \approx 1.21$$

The output is HIGH for about 1.21 times as long as it is LOW.

Reading an Oscilloscope Trace

An oscilloscope displays voltage on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. Two key controls determine the scale: volts per division (V/div) and time per division (time/div or timebase).

To read a 555 astable output waveform from an oscilloscope trace:

  1. Amplitude: Count the number of vertical divisions from the bottom of the waveform to the top of the HIGH level. Multiply by V/div. This is the amplitude of the waveform. Do not confuse amplitude with peak-to-peak voltage — for a waveform that swings between 0 V and +9 V, the amplitude is 9 V and the peak-to-peak voltage is also 9 V (but for a waveform centred on 0 V, peak-to-peak is twice the amplitude).
  2. Period: Count the number of horizontal divisions for one complete cycle (one HIGH + one LOW). Multiply by time/div. This gives the period \(T\) in seconds (or ms or μs, depending on the timebase setting).
  3. Frequency: \(f = 1/T\). If \(T\) was measured in ms, convert to seconds before dividing: \(1\) ms \(= 10^{-3}\) s.
Key Fact

Amplitude is measured in volts (V), not milliseconds. Period is measured in time (s, ms, or μs), not volts. These unit errors are the most common mistake in oscilloscope questions. Always state the V/div and time/div values before reading off measurements.

Examiner reports identify 555 astable questions as among the worst-performing on both papers. The most frequent mistakes are:

  • Mishandling the k and μ multipliers: \(R = 47\) kΩ must be entered as \(47 \times 10^3\) or \(47{,}000\) Ω in the formula — not as \(47\).
  • Multiplying \(R_1\) by 2 instead of \(R_2\): the formula is \(R_1 + 2R_2\), so \(R_2\) gets the factor of 2, not \(R_1\).
  • Giving amplitude in ms or period in V — this is a category error. Amplitude is always in volts; period is always in time units.
  • Confusing peak-to-peak and amplitude for waveforms that swing symmetrically around 0 V.
exam_tip_html: In the frequency formula \(f = 1.44 / [(R_1 + 2R_2)C]\), note that \(R_2\) is multiplied by 2 — not \(R_1\). Always convert resistors to ohms and capacitors to farads before substituting. On oscilloscope questions, state the time/div before reading the period, and the V/div before reading the amplitude — then give amplitude in volts and period in seconds or milliseconds (never the wrong unit for the wrong quantity).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 555 astable oscillates continuously; frequency is \(f = 1.44 / [(R_1 + 2R_2)C]\) where \(R_2\) carries the factor of 2.
  • Mark-space ratio \(= T_{ON} / T_{OFF} = (R_1 + R_2) / R_2\); it is always > 1 in a standard astable and equals the duty cycle above 50%.
  • On an oscilloscope, amplitude is read in volts (vertical divisions × V/div) and period in time (horizontal divisions × time/div) — never swap the units.

practice_questions.text:
A 555 astable has R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ and C = 100 nF. What is its output frequency?
A) 480 Hz
B) 720 Hz
C) 1440 Hz
D) 144 Hz
State the meaning of mark-space ratio for a rectangular waveform.
practice_questions.marks: The ratio of the time the output is HIGH (mark time) [1] to the time it is LOW (space time) [1].

practice_questions.text:
An oscilloscope displays a 555 astable output waveform. The timebase is set to 2 ms/div and the volts/div is 2 V/div. One complete cycle occupies 4 horizontal divisions and the waveform rises from 0 V to a height of 3 vertical divisions.
(a) State the period of the waveform. [1 mark]
(b) Calculate the frequency. [1 mark]
(c) State the amplitude. [1 mark]
practice_questions.type: 3 marks — Read Off Graph or Oscilloscope
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Period = \(4 \times 2\) ms = 8 ms [1].
(b) \(f = 1 / 0.008 = 125\) Hz [1].
(c) Amplitude = \(3 \times 2\) V = 6 V [1].

practice_questions.text:
A 555 astable LED flasher uses R1 = 22 kΩ, R2 = 47 kΩ and C = 10 μF.
(a) Calculate the frequency of the output. [2 marks]
(b) Calculate the mark-space ratio. [2 marks]

Design a 555 astable circuit to produce an output frequency of approximately 500 Hz with a mark-space ratio as close to 1:1 as possible. A 100 nF capacitor is available. Determine suitable values for R1 and R2. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: For 500 Hz: \(R_1 + 2R_2 = 1.44 / (500 \times 100 \times 10^{-9}) = 1.44 / (5 \times 10^{-5}) = 28{,}800\) Ω [1]. To make mark-space ratio close to 1, minimise \(R_1\) (a standard 555 cannot achieve exactly 1:1) [1]. Choose \(R_1 = 1\) kΩ [1]; then \(2R_2 \approx 27{,}800\) Ω so \(R_2 \approx 13{,}900\) Ω — use 15 kΩ (nearest E24) [1]. Check: \(f = 1.44 / [(1{,}000 + 30{,}000) \times 10^{-7}] = 1.44 / 0.0031 \approx 465\) Hz; mark-space = \((1+15)/15 = 1.07\) which is close to 1:1 [1].

practice_questions.text:
A 555 astable circuit is being used to drive a piezo sounder as part of a fire alarm. R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ and C = 47 nF.
(a) Calculate the output frequency. [2 marks]
(b) A technician says increasing R2 to 22 kΩ will make the alarm sound lower. Evaluate whether this is correct. [3 marks]
(c) The oscilloscope shows the output waveform has a peak of 3.5 divisions with the V/div set to 2 V/div. State the amplitude. [1 mark]
(d) The timebase is 0.5 ms/div and one full cycle spans 4.5 divisions. Calculate the frequency from the oscilloscope and compare with the calculated value. [2 marks]
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Circuit Analysis and Evaluation
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: (a) f = 1.44/[(1000 + 20000) × 47 × 10⁻⁹] = 1.44/[21000 × 47 × 10⁻⁹] = 1.44/9.87 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 1459 Hz; (b) with R2 = 22 kΩ: f = 1.44/[(1000 + 44000) × 47 × 10⁻⁹] = 1.44/2.115 × 10⁻³ ≈ 681 Hz — lower frequency, so the alarm does sound lower; the technician is correct; (c) amplitude = 3.5 × 2 = 7 V; (d) period = 4.5 × 0.5 ms = 2.25 ms, f = 1/0.00225 ≈ 444 Hz — lower than calculated (1459 Hz suggests the capacitor may differ or timebase misread — students should note discrepancy.
Secure: (a), (c) correct; (b) logic correct but imprecise; (d) period calculated but comparison missed.
Developing: Frequency formula applied; unit error in multiplier for C or R.
Emerging: Only period from oscilloscope correctly calculated.

knowledge_checks.q: In the 555 astable frequency formula, which resistor is multiplied by 2?
In a 555 astable, the output is always HIGH for longer than it is LOW. This is because the capacitor charges through:
options: R1 and R2 in series, but discharges through R2 only

knowledge_checks.q: Amplitude on an oscilloscope is measured in _____, not milliseconds.
The ratio of T_ON to T_OFF in a repeating waveform is called the _____ ratio.
Match each 555 astable quantity to its formula:

flashcard_questions.q: What is the 555 astable frequency formula?
In the 555 astable formula, which resistor gets the factor of 2?
What is the mark-space ratio formula for a 555 astable?
Can a standard 555 astable produce a 1:1 mark-space ratio (50% duty cycle)?
flashcard_questions.a: No — R1 > 0 means T_ON is always greater than T_OFF.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the timebase (time/div) control on an oscilloscope tell you?
flashcard_questions.a: The time represented by each horizontal division.

flashcard_questions.q: How do you calculate frequency from an oscilloscope trace?
flashcard_questions.a: Measure period T (horizontal divs × time/div), then f = 1/T.

flashcard_questions.q: A 555 astable has R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ, C = 100 nF. What is f?

flashcard_questions.a: The fraction of one cycle the output is HIGH, expressed as a percentage.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is it wrong to give period in volts or amplitude in milliseconds?
flashcard_questions.a: Period is a time measurement (seconds/ms); amplitude is a voltage measurement (volts) — they are different physical quantities.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to the 555 astable frequency if R2 is increased while R1 and C stay constant?
flashcard_questions.a: Frequency decreases (denominator increases, so f = 1.44/[(R1+2R2)C] gets smaller).

glossary_terms.definition: A 555 timer operating mode that oscillates continuously without any trigger, producing a repeating square-wave output.
A circuit that produces a continuously repeating electrical signal, usually a square or rectangular wave.
The ratio of the time the output is HIGH (mark) to the time the output is LOW (space) in a repeating waveform.
The fraction of one complete cycle during which the output is HIGH, expressed as a percentage.
The voltage represented by each vertical division on the oscilloscope screen, set by the volts/div control.
The time represented by each horizontal division on the oscilloscope screen, set by the time/div or timebase control.
